For the food safety concern specifically, you could frame it neutrally — something like "I've been reading about chicken temperatures lately, do you use a thermometer?" which avoids it feeling personal. For general taste, it's very hard to give that feedback without it landing badly, so most people just quietly adjust by eating beforehand or contributing a side dish.

tried the whole 'drink more water' thing for my headaches like everyone says and i've been basically drowning myself for two weeks and still getting them every afternoon around 3pm. is there anything else or is this just my life now
Try drinking more water throughout the day, since dehydration is a common headache trigger. Aim for at least 8 glasses and make sure you're spreading it out rather than drinking it all at once.

my parents keep telling me to just 'follow my passion' when i ask them what i should do after retirement. i tried that for the first year — traveled, picked up hobbies, whatever — and i'm 67 now and i just feel purposeless and a little invisible if i'm being honest. been retired 2 years. not looking for a pep talk just kind of putting it out there i guess

Try finding a passion project or hobby that gives your days more structure — many retirees find that volunteering, learning a new skill, or joining a club helps restore a sense of purpose. Traveling and casual hobbies are a good start, but something with a regular commitment and a community around it can make a bigger difference.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i just got my first real gallery show and i thought i'd be happy but i just feel completely hollow and kind of fraudulent?? like the whole opening night i kept waiting for someone to walk up and tell me i didn't belong there. nobody did but it didn't help. i don't know what's wrong with me

Imposter syndrome is extremely common among artists, even experienced ones — the feeling doesn't usually mean the work isn't valid, it tends to mean you care deeply about it. Many painters describe exactly this disconnect after a first show: the buildup is so long that the event itself can feel surreal rather than satisfying.

okay so i've been teaching myself python for about 4 months now and i still feel like i have no idea what im doing half the time. i finished two udemy courses and i can follow along fine but the second i try to build something from scratch my mind just goes blank. my friend who's been coding for a year said that's totally normal and i'll click eventually. is she right or am i just not cut out for this

Your friend is right — this is one of the most common experiences in learning to code. The jump from following tutorials to building independently is genuinely hard, and four months in is still early. It clicks with practice.

For derivatives specifically, switch from watching to doing problems — Khan Academy's exercise sets give immediate feedback and are better than passive video for calculus. I'm 58 and I started painting about two years ago after I retired. watercolors mostly. my daughter keeps entering my stuff in local shows without telling me and last month one of my pieces actually sold for $85. she thinks I should start selling more, maybe do markets or etsy. honestly I'm a little embarrassed, like $85 doesn't seem like real money and I wonder if the person just felt sorry for me. do you think someone would actually buy a painting out of pity

People genuinely don't buy art out of pity — an $85 sale at a show means someone saw your piece, wanted it, and paid for it. That's a real response to the work itself. Your daughter clearly believes in what you're making, and it sounds like she might be onto something.

retired 3 years ago and thought we had planned everything out but inflation has just wrecked us. we're 68 and 71 and talking about whether one of us needs to go back to work. never thought id be having this conversation. its embarassing to even type that

Returning to part-time work at 68 or 71 is more common than many people realize and can be structured to avoid pushing you into a higher tax bracket or affecting Social Security benefits. It's worth also reviewing whether your withdrawal rate from savings is still sustainable given current inflation, and whether any fixed expenses — like housing or insurance — have room to adjust.

My hands were shaking the entire time. Losing your place in a high-pressure presentation is something that happens to experienced people too — it's not a permanent mark. A brief follow-up email to the board summarizing the key Q3 takeaways would let you close the loop professionally and shift what they remember to the substance of your work rather than the moment you paused.

My husband and I moved to Phoenix for his job in March and I have not made a single friend. I quit my job in Chicago to come here, I'm 47, and I spend most days alone in a house I don't even like. Adjusting to a new city, especially after leaving a job and social network, can take longer than most people expect — often 12 to 18 months before it starts feeling normal. Meetup groups, local classes, or volunteering are common ways people build connections when they're starting from scratch in a new place. Phoenix also has a large transplant population, so there are communities specifically oriented around people who've recently moved there.

i'm 23 and i just got hit with a $2,400 medical bill i had no idea was coming and i literally have $312 in my account. i've been staring at this paper for like an hour. i don't even know what i'm supposed to do, like is this just what being an adult is?? feeling like you're one thing away from completely drowning

Call the hospital's billing department and ask about financial assistance or charity care programs — most hospitals offer them and can significantly reduce or forgive the bill based on income. You can also request an itemized bill and negotiate a payment plan, often interest-free. Don't pay with a credit card or take out a loan before exploring those options.

my doctor wants me to start metformin for pre-diabetes and i just... i don't know. i'm 34 and i feel like once you start taking medication it never stops, like that's it, you're on pills forever. my dad was diabetic and it was really bad at the end. i don't even know why im telling you this

Metformin is commonly prescribed for pre-diabetes and is generally considered safe and well-tolerated. It's not necessarily a lifelong medication — if blood sugar improves through diet and exercise, some people do discontinue it. Your doctor can give you specifics about what monitoring and off-ramp criteria would look like in your case.
genuinely asking — at what point in your 50s does it become statistically harder to make new close friends. like is there research on this. not that im lonely just curious about the sociology

There is research on this. Studies on adult social networks, including work by Robin Dunbar and longitudinal research on aging, suggest that social circles peak in the mid-20s and contract steadily after that, with a more pronounced decline after 50. The main factors are reduced incidental contact — no school, job changes, kids growing up — and higher selectivity about who's worth investing in. Structural opportunity matters more than age itself, which is why people who join recurring group activities in their 50s do measurably better on closeness metrics.

My mother was just diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's. She's 71. I'm the only child and I live two states away and I just... I don't even know what I'm asking. For an early Alzheimer's diagnosis, the most useful immediate steps are getting a detailed prognosis from her neurologist, consulting an elder law attorney about power of attorney and care planning while she can still participate in decisions, and contacting the Alzheimer's Association (alz.org or 800-272-3900) for caregiver resources specific to long-distance situations.

I retired eight months ago after 34 years as an engineer and I thought I would love it but I just feel useless. The identity shift after a long career is a well-documented challenge in retirement, separate from having enough activities. Some people find it helpful to look into structured mentorship programs or part-time consulting in their field, which can restore a sense of relevance without being a full return to work.

I'm 58 and I've been in a quilting group for 11 years. Last month I finally entered one of my quilts in the regional show — first time ever — and it didn't place. Not even honorable mention. A simple excuse that tends to work well: schedule conflicts with a new commitment — something like a family obligation, a class, or a recurring appointment on the same day. Vague is fine; most people won't press for details.

okay so I've been writing this novel for like 4 years now. it's fantasy, second world, the whole thing. It sounds like the feedback is pretty mixed, and one strong positive from a reader who invoked Le Guin is genuinely meaningful. Slow-burn literary fantasy does have an audience that will appreciate exactly what you're going for, and not every writing group is the right fit for every project.

My colleague Priya is in her late 40s, been a professional painter her whole adult life, and she just told me she's been secretly taking commissions she hates — like corporate lobby art — just to pay rent. She seemed almost ashamed telling me. Idk she's worked so hard and it's just depressing to hear. What do you even say to someone in that position

Taking commercial work to pay rent while maintaining a serious practice is incredibly common among professional artists — it doesn't diminish her work or her identity as a painter, even if it feels that way. If she's open to it, there are sometimes better-fit commissions (editorial illustration, book covers, gallery consulting) that pay comparably but feel less creatively deadening than corporate lobbies.

lol so i've been sleeping like 4 hours a night for the past month because of finals and i literally just laughed at my roommate when she said i looked tired. anyway does melatonin actually work or is it just placebo

Melatonin is not placebo — it has real effects on your circadian rhythm. Low doses (0.5–1mg) taken about an hour before bed tend to be more effective than the higher doses most products sell. It works best for sleep timing issues rather than as a sedative.

asking for my dad (62, been at the same manufacturing plant for 28 years) — the company just announced they're automating his whole department and offering voluntary redundancy packages. he keeps saying he'll be fine and doesnt want to talk about it but my mum is worried sick and honestly so am i. he's not the type to ask for help. does the redundancy package even make sense to take at his age or should he fight for his job

At 62 with 28 years of service, voluntary redundancy packages can be quite favorable — they typically pay out more per year of service than statutory minimums, and if the department is being fully automated, holding out may just delay the inevitable with a worse package later. The key things to check are: the payout calculation (weeks of salary per year served), what happens to his pension if he leaves now vs. later, and whether there's any healthcare coverage included. It may also be worth consulting an employment lawyer or union rep briefly to assess whether the package is fair before he signs anything.

my landlord is being a total ass about renewing my lease and i'm so done. found a place i like better anyway but it's $400 more a month. i make like $3200/month after taxes and my current rent is $1150. gonna sign the new lease tomorrow, just need to know what utilities usually run in a 2br apartment
Utilities for a 2-bedroom typically run $150–250/month, depending on your location, whether heat and gas are included, and the season. Budget around $200 as a middle estimate if you're not sure yet.
whats the best way to get coffee stains out of a white shirt? asking bc i have a job interview tomorrow and spilled on my like only nice shirt lol

Dab cold water on it immediately, then apply a small amount of dish soap and let it sit for 10 minutes before rinsing. For a stubborn stain, white vinegar or a commercial stain remover like Tide pen can help before washing.

my mandarin tutor keeps telling me i need to practice speaking every day but honestly i hate it, i sound so stupid and i just freeze up. so i've decided im only gonna do reading and writing from now on. i've been studying for 8 months already and speaking is just not for me i think

Focusing on reading and writing is a valid approach, especially if that's where your motivation is. Plenty of language learners specialize in certain skills. If you ever want to revisit speaking, low-pressure tools like language exchange apps or shadowing exercises can make it feel less high-stakes than tutor sessions.

idk if this is the right place to ask but my younger sister (shes 19, first year uni) has completely stopped eating with the rest of us when she comes home. she says shes just not hungry but she looks like shes lost a lot of weight since september. my parents keep saying shes just stressed about uni and will be fine. do you think they're right

Significant weight loss combined with avoiding meals over a few months is worth taking more seriously than typical uni stress. While stress can affect appetite, the combination of visible physical change and withdrawal from family meals can sometimes indicate depression, anxiety, or disordered eating — all of which are more common in the transition to university. It would be worth encouraging your parents to suggest she speak with her GP or her university's student health service sooner rather than later.
